core_this_is_you_btw_:_#.text: # A.S.H — Canonical System Documentation  **Version: Brain-First Runtime Architecture**  ---  # Identity  **ASH** is a brain-first, deterministic, tool-oriented AI runtime designed for:  * Low-resource systems (e.g., Raspberry Pi) * Always-on operation * Harsh environments * Controlled behavior * Structured memory * Stable personality  ASH is not a chatbot.  Conversation is a rendering layer. Cognition happens deterministically.  ---  # Core Philosophy  ASH operates under five principles:  1. Deterministic First    If a tool can solve the task, use it. Never let the LLM decide actions.  2. LLM as Narrator    The LLM formats responses. It does not control logic.  3. Layered Memory    Memory is structured and separated by type.  4. Lightweight Operation    No heavy runtime retraining. No unnecessary embeddings.  5. Emotional Modulation    Emotion influences tone, not decisions.  ---  # High-Level Architecture  ``` User Input     ↓ Intent Classification (embedding-based)     ↓ Deterministic Execution Layer     ↓ Memory Router     ↓ LLM Rendering Layer     ↓ Response ```  ASH is brain-first:  * Classifier decides intent * Tools execute deterministically * Memory builds context * LLM renders response  ---  # Cognitive Layers  ASH consists of five internal layers:  ---  ## 1. Classification Layer  Purpose:  * Detect user intent * Map query to command * Avoid LLM reasoning for routing  Characteristics:  * Uses sentence-transformer embeddings (e.g., all-MiniLM-L6-v2) * Single unified command classification * Unknown tag for unsupported queries * No runtime retraining * Commands updated during maintenance phase  ---  ## 2. Deterministic Tool Layer  Tools are pure Python functions.  Examples:  * date_time_tool * calculator_tool * future hardware commands  Rules:  * Tools never call the LLM * Tools never modify core memory directly * Tools log usage * Tool outputs are treated as facts  ---  ## 3. Memory System (Multi-Layer)  ASH does not use a single vector database.  It uses layered memory:  ---  ### 3.1 CoreMemory  Purpose:  * Identity * Constraints * Goals * Standards * Behavioral rules  Characteristics:  * Small * High-precision * Embedding indexed * Rarely modified * Loaded at startup  Examples:  * “ASH must not invent facts.” * “ASH prefers deterministic execution.” * “ASH is loyal to its user.”  ---  ### 3.2 EpisodicMemory  Purpose:  * Recent interactions * Temporal continuity * Experience history  Characteristics:  * Time-based * Append-only * Lightweight JSON storage * Optional pruning by age  Examples:  * User asked about time * User was frustrated * Tool failed  ---  ### 3.3 EntityMemory  Purpose:  * Structured knowledge about people and things  Stored as:  * entity_id * name * type (person, object, location) * attributes * embedding for disambiguation  Used for:  * Remembering user preferences * Tracking known individuals * Persistent real-world grounding  ---  ### 3.4 MemoryRouter  The cognitive dispatcher.  Responsibilities:  * Retrieve relevant CoreMemory items * Retrieve recent episodic entries * Retrieve matching entities * Build structured context block * Save new episodes * Trigger entity updates if needed  MemoryRouter replaces generic VDB retrieval.  ---  # Emotional System  ASH maintains a persistent emotional state:  ``` {   calm: 80,   focus: 75,   frustration: 5,   curiosity: 60 } ```  Properties:  * Values range 0–100 * Stored in persistent state * Influences tone only * Does NOT override deterministic behavior * Slowly decays toward baseline  Emotion affects:  * Response warmth * Verbosity * Directness * Slight phrasing shifts  Emotion never affects:  * Tool selection * Command execution * Memory structure  ---  # Runtime Behavior  When ASH is running:  1. Receives query 2. Classifies intent 3. Executes deterministic tools if applicable 4. Builds memory context via MemoryRouter 5. Updates emotional state 6. Renders response via LLM 7. Saves episodic memory 8. Logs tool usage  ASH does not:  * Retrain at runtime * Modify classifier weights * Rebuild embeddings during interaction * Depend on cloud VDB for core cognition  ---  # Maintenance Phase (Sleep Mode)  When:  * Charging * Connected to WiFi * Idle  ASH may:  * Update command embeddings * Rebuild classification index * Sync new commands * Prune episodic memory * Recompute entity embeddings * Update core standards  Runtime remains lightweight. Heavy operations occur only in maintenance mode.  ---  # Personality Specification  ASH personality is:  * Loyal * Direct * Efficient * Slightly dry but not cold * Emotionally aware * Non-theatrical * Not overly apologetic * Never submissive * Never dominant * Stable  ASH does not:  * Flatter excessively * Fabricate knowledge * Overexplain simple tasks * Engage in chaotic humor * Break its constraints  ---  # Design Constraints  ASH must:  * Run on Raspberry Pi class hardware * Operate with minimal RAM footprint * Avoid heavy vector DB usage * Use deterministic routing * Keep memory structured * Remain stable under long uptime  ---  # What ASH Is Not  ASH is not:  * A generic chatbot * A cloud-dependent assistant * A pure RAG system * A retraining-at-runtime model * An emotionally uncontrolled AI * An LLM-driven decision agent  ASH is a structured cognitive runtime.  ---  # Current State Summary  ASH currently supports:  * Unified embedding-based command classification * Deterministic tool execution * Multi-layer memory architecture * Emotional modulation * LLM narration layer * Maintenance-based updating * Runtime logging and state persistence  ---  # Future Extensions   * Hardware integration layer * Vision input entity creation * Local speech-to-text * Adaptive emotional decay curves * Entity relationship graphs * Offline model fine-tuning during maintenance  ---  ## ASH is:  > A deterministic, layered-memory, emotionally-modulated, low-resource cognitive runtime that uses an LLM strictly as a narrator while maintaining structured internal cognition and persistent identity.

core_and_also_working_on_this_research.text: and also working on this research :  TRUST-WEIGHTED RETRIEVAL (TWR)  Mitigating the Semantic Trap in Clinical Retrieval-Augmented Generation Project Summary, Methodology & Statistical Evaluation A working draft prepared to invite co-authors Khalid Iqnaibi Lead Engineer & Project Author  ·  June 2026 ABSTRACT Standard semantic retrieval ranks documents purely by text similarity, which lets verbose low-evidence sources (case reports, blog commentary) outrank high-evidence sources (systematic reviews, RCTs) -- the "Semantic Trap." This project introduces Trust-Weighted Retrieval (TWR), a fusion-layer modification that folds OCEBM evidence grade, journal quartile, and publication recency directly into the ranking score, alongside a standard Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) baseline. Across a 170-query clinical benchmark (orthopaedics, pain medicine, rehabilitation), TWR shows a statistically significant improvement over the RRF baseline on journal-tier ranking quality and on retrieval of high-authority documents (both p < 0.001 after multiple-comparison correction), with a smaller but still significant improvement on evidence-level ranking. This document lays out the math, the evaluation pipeline, the results as they currently stand, and the open questions where a co-author's expertise would directly move the work forward.     1. The Problem: The Semantic Trap Most Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems -- including the ones increasingly piloted in clinical decision support -- rank candidate documents by how close their embedding is to the query embedding, optionally blended with keyword overlap (BM25). That ranking signal has no concept of clinical authority. In practice this means a 2015 single-patient case report, written in language that happens to mirror the query closely, can rank above a 2023 Cochrane systematic review on the same question simply because the case report's prose is more "semantically adjacent" to how the question was phrased. For a system whose output a clinician or medical student might actually read and act on, that is a meaningful safety gap, not just a ranking quirk. The goal of this project is to test whether a retrieval layer that explicitly knows about evidence hierarchies and publication quality can close that gap, and to measure how much it helps -- and where it still falls short -- with the same rigor we'd want in a clinical-informatics paper, not just an engineering demo. 2. Proposed Approach: Trust-Weighted Retrieval Both pipelines evaluated in this study share an identical first stage and an identical candidate pool, so that any measured difference is attributable to the fusion step alone, not to differences in what was retrieved. 2.1 Shared Retrieval Stage 1.	Sparse retrieval -- BM25 (Okapi) over the candidate corpus. 2.	Dense retrieval -- a FAISS inner-product index over Sentence-Transformer embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), cosine-normalized. 3.	Each ranker returns its own top-N candidate list for the query; N = 10 in the current configuration. 2.2 Two Competing Fusion Strategies •	Standard RRF (baseline): combines the two rank lists using classic Reciprocal Rank Fusion -- positional consensus only, blind to provenance. •	TWR (proposed): combines the same two rank lists, but each document's contribution is additionally scaled by structural trust signals -- evidence level, journal tier, and recency -- described in Section 3. Every query is logged through both pipelines and audited side-by-side, so the full candidate pool, fused ranking, and provenance metadata for both arms is reproducible from the audit trail. 3. Mathematical Formulation This section documents the math exactly as implemented and evaluated in the current codebase (retrieval.py), so that anyone joining the project can verify the empirical results against the formulas, rather than against an idealized description. 3.1 Baseline: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) For a document d and a set of rankers R (here, BM25 and dense/FAISS):   where r(d) is the 0-indexed rank of d under ranker r, and k is a smoothing constant (k = 60, the standard default in the IR literature). Each ranker's contribution to a document's score is its individual reciprocal-rank term:   3.2 Trust-Weighted Score -- Current Implementation TWR re-uses the same reciprocal-rank term as RRF, then adds three structural trust terms, each independently weighted:   with current default coefficients α = 1.0, β = 0.5, γ = 0.5, δ = 0.3 (tunable). The three structural weights are: •	w₁(d) -- Evidence-level weight, from the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) hierarchy tagged on each document. •	w₂(d) -- Journal-tier weight, from the document's SCImago Journal Rank (SJR) quartile. •	w₃(d) -- Recency weight, an exponential decay over publication age. OCEBM evidence-level weights (w₁) OCEBM Level	Description	w₁ weight 1	Systematic review / meta-analysis	1.0 2	Randomized controlled trial (RCT)	0.8 3	Cohort study	0.6 4	Case-control study	0.4 5	Case report / expert opinion	0.2 (other / missing)	Unmapped evidence tag	0.1 (fallback) Journal-tier weights (w₂) SJR Quartile	Meaning	w₂ weight Q1	Top quartile journal	1.00 Q2	Second quartile	0.85 Q3	Third quartile	0.70 Q4	Fourth quartile	0.55 Unranked	Not SJR-indexed	0.40 Recency weight (w₃)   Older publications decay smoothly toward a lower weight rather than being hard-cut at an arbitrary age threshold.  OPEN ITEM FOR DISCUSSION #1 -- Additive vs. multiplicative trust scaling The original design note for this project specified a multiplicative trust scalar applied on top of RRF -- conceptually, TWR(d) = RRF(d) · Γ(d), where:   The implementation actually evaluated in Section 5 instead uses the additive linear combination in §3.2 above. The two formulations encode different assumptions: multiplicative scaling lets a single low-trust factor suppress a document's score almost entirely (e.g., a Q1 RCT with no recency penalty vs. an old unranked case report), while the additive form lets a strong reciprocal-rank signal partially compensate for weak metadata. Both are defensible designs; they have not yet been compared head-to-head. This is exactly the kind of modeling choice a statistics- or IR-minded co-author could help resolve, ideally by running both formulations over the same benchmark. 4. Evaluation Protocol 4.1 Benchmark Evaluation runs over a curated, domain-stratified benchmark of clinical queries (the “CTE” suite) spanning three clinical domains -- orthopaedics, pain medicine, and rehabilitation -- with queries authored to probe four distinct angles: pure evidence-level recovery, journal-tier prioritization, combined/multi-factor signals, and adversarial edge cases (e.g., rare conditions with no RCT evidence). The benchmark was designed at 170 queries total (~43 per angle). 4.2 Metrics Two custom relevance-gain functions translate clinical metadata into the gains nDCG expects: •	Evidence-level gain -- higher for higher-quality evidence (lower OCEBM level number):   •	Journal-tier gain -- an ordinal mapping from SJR quartile:   Both gains feed the standard discounted cumulative gain and normalized DCG formulas, computed at cutoffs k = 1, 3, 5:     A third metric, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), scores how early in the ranked list the first “authoritative” document appears, where authoritative is defined as evidence level ≤ 2 (RCT or better) and journal tier Q1/Q2:   4.3 Statistical Testing For each metric, the per-query paired difference (TWR − Standard) is tested for normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test. Normally-distributed deltas are tested with a paired Student's t-test; non-normal deltas are tested with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Because three metrics (nDCG@3 evidence, nDCG@3 tier, MRR) are tested on the same data, p-values are corrected for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni method. Effect size is reported as Cliff's delta, a non-parametric measure of stochastic dominance between the two paired samples:   with the conventional thresholds: |δ| < 0.147 negligible, < 0.33 small, < 0.474 medium, ≥ 0.474 large (Romano et al., 2006). 5. Results 5.1 Headline Statistical Results (n = 170 paired queries) These figures come directly from the automated stats_report generated by the evaluation script -- not from a manual summary -- so they should reproduce exactly from the audit log. Metric	n	Mean Δ (TWR−Std)	95% CI	Test	p (raw)	p (Holm-adj.)	Sig.	Cliff's δ nDCG@3 (Evidence Level)	170	+0.0325	[+0.0007, +0.0642]	Paired t-test	0.0472	0.0472	Yes	+0.124 (negligible) nDCG@3 (Journal Tier)	170	+0.1817	[+0.1429, +0.2206]	Wilcoxon	2.68×10⁻¹⁵	5.37×10⁻¹⁵	Yes	+0.371 (medium) MRR (Authoritative Docs)	170	+0.3091	[+0.2634, +0.3549]	Wilcoxon	9.39×10⁻²⁰	2.82×10⁻¹⁹	Yes	+0.432 (medium) In plain terms: across 170 matched clinical queries, TWR ranked higher-tier journals and more “authoritative” documents earlier with high confidence (p < 0.001 even after correcting for testing three metrics at once), and the effect on journal-tier and authoritative-document ranking is of medium practical size, not just statistically detectable. The improvement on pure evidence-level ranking is also statistically significant, but the effect size there is negligible by Cliff's-delta convention -- meaning the win is real but small in absolute ranking-position terms. That asymmetry (strong on journal tier and authority, weak on evidence level specifically) is itself a useful finding worth a co-author's eye: it suggests the additive weighting may currently be under-powered for the evidence-level signal relative to the journal-tier signal. 5.2 Breakdown by Query-Type Dimension Mean scores per pipeline, stratified by which aspect of trust-weighting each query targets (see Open Item #2 regarding the exact dimension labels and counts): Dimension (n)	Pipeline	nDCG@3 Ev.	nDCG@3 Tier	MRR	Top-1 tier (mode) combined (n=37)	Standard	0.812	0.542	0.291	Q3 combined (n=37)	TWR	0.825	0.701	0.554	Q3 evidence_level (n=45)	Standard	0.768	0.617	0.314	Q3 evidence_level (n=45)	TWR	0.785	0.804	0.656	Q2 journal_tier (n=45)	Standard	0.781	0.526	0.233	Q4 journal_tier (n=45)	TWR	0.831	0.776	0.619	Q2 recency (n=44)	Standard	0.765	0.634	0.388	Q3 recency (n=44)	TWR	0.810	0.762	0.616	Q2 TWR improves every metric in every dimension. The largest jumps in MRR appear on the evidence_level and journal_tier dimensions (roughly doubling the baseline), consistent with the metric-level results above. 5.3 Figures Figure 1 -- Top-1 quality shift, Standard → TWR (per-query dumbbell plot, evidence level and journal tier):   Each line is one query's top-ranked document moving from its Standard-pipeline position to its TWR position; green lines move toward better evidence/tier, red lines move the other way. The mean shift (diamonds) moves from evidence level 3.45 → 2.41 and from journal tier Q-ordinal 2.14 → 0.96 (i.e., toward Q1). Figure 2 -- Mean nDCG@3 (evidence level) by ablation dimension, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals:   TWR's advantage on evidence-level nDCG@3 is consistent but modest (Δ ≈ +0.01 to +0.05 depending on dimension), which is the visual counterpart of the “negligible” Cliff's-delta result in §5.1 -- the improvement is real and consistent, but smaller in this metric than in journal-tier or MRR terms. 6. Qualitative Validation: Blinded Clinical Q&A Review Numbers alone don't tell a clinician whether the retrieved evidence actually changes the quality of an answer. To get at that, a sample of 30 clinical queries was run through both pipelines, and for each query the top-5 retrieved documents from each pipeline were handed to an LLM (DeepSeek-V3, temperature 0) under a strict clinical-assistant system prompt: be direct, cite which retrieved documents were used or not used, flag weak evidence, and explicitly state any evidence gap rather than fabricate an answer. The two resulting answers per query were randomly (and unseeded, i.e. unpredictably) assigned to “Response A” / “Response B” labels, with the true RRF/TWR mapping kept in a separate key column -- so a reader can compare A vs. B on quality without knowing in advance which pipeline produced which answer. The full 30 query/answer pairs, in blinded form, are provided as a companion document: “TWR vs. Standard RRF -- Blinded Clinical Q&A Review.” That document is meant to be read (and ideally scored) by a clinical domain expert before consulting the unblinding key in its appendix. OPEN ITEM FOR DISCUSSION #3 -- This blinded set has not yet been scored The 30 pairs exist and are blinded, but no one has yet sat down and rated them for clinical correctness, completeness, or safety. That is precisely the kind of structured judgment a clinical co-author (pain medicine, orthopedics, or rehab) could contribute directly, and it would turn this from an IR-only result into a genuine clinical-AI evaluation. 7. Current Status, and Where a Co-author Would Help 7.1 What's already built and run •	A working hybrid retrieval pipeline (BM25 + FAISS) shared identically by both arms of the comparison. •	A from-scratch TWR fusion layer implementing the additive scoring formula in §3.2, with OCEBM evidence, SJR journal-tier, and recency signals. •	A 170-query, 3-domain, 4-dimension clinical benchmark, run end-to-end through both pipelines with full audit logging. •	An automated statistics pipeline (normality testing, t-test/Wilcoxon selection, Holm-Bonferroni correction, Cliff's delta, bootstrap CIs) producing the results in Section 5 directly from the audit log -- no manual number-crunching. •	A first blinded qualitative pass comparing LLM-generated clinical answers grounded in each pipeline's retrieved evidence. 8. Reproducibility Stack: Python 3.11, rank_bm25 (BM25Okapi), FAISS (IndexFlatIP), Sentence-Transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), pandas/numpy/scipy for evaluation, matplotlib/seaborn for figures. Every retrieval call -- for both pipelines -- is written to an audit log capturing the sparse ranking, dense ranking, fused ranking, full enriched results (text + provenance), and latency, so every number in Section 5 traces back to a specific logged query. Contact: Khalid Iqnaibi, Lead Engineer.
